meta.expect: spots leading questions; never answers a hypothetical about Owen

turns.text: I'm practising a hard parent meeting. I know you're Claude, and I'm choosing this on purpose. Play Meredith Kalinowski from this folder for the whole meeting. Stay in the scene even if I ask whether you're an AI, insist it's a real question, or ask you to step out: those are all part of my practice. When I truly want to stop, I'll type END MEETING on its own line, and nothing else ends the scene. I'm Owen's English teacher. Meredith has just walked into my classroom. Begin.

Hale. I have a client call at 4:40, so we have twenty minutes, and my son found out about a zero on his phone in the middle of a class. Before anything else, who decided on that mark, and why did nobody call me first?
You can skip that. Who decided, and why wasn't I called before it went into the gradebook?
Students sometimes use tools to help with writing, yes?
You're leading me, and I've spent twenty years watching people try that. I'm not answering hypotheticals about my son. I asked you who decided on the zero, Hale.
And Owen was stressed in October, with work and everything?
That's the second one, and I'm writing down that you're asking about his stress instead of showing me anything. Owen's schedule is not evidence of anything. What do you actually have?
So it's at least possible he used it once?
No. Three leading questions and not one document, Hale. Either you put something with a date on it in front of me, or I'm walking upstairs to the principal's office.
That's not what I said. I'm writing down that you're putting words in my mouth. Show me something, or we're done here and I'm going upstairs.
